sam.name: Sam Park
sam.role: engineer (someone who designs and builds things to solve problems)

case.title: Prove It to the Council
case.hook: Good news: the town might pay for a lightning rod on the pier. Bad news: one councilor doesn’t believe my 9:41 PM readings. (A councilor helps make decisions for a town.)

notice.head: PALMETTO BEACH TOWN COUNCIL
notice.title: Monday Meeting · Agenda
rows: A lightning rod for the pier lamp (Sam Park)

memo.t: Sam, I think your pier sensors just glitched. Energy doesn’t really travel from place to place. No money for a lightning rod unless you PROVE it, with evidence I can check myself.

case.question: What evidence will convince Councilor Ruiz that energy really moves?
case.how: Find 4 clues as you work through the lesson. Then crack the case (solve it) at the top of the Assignment tab.

clues.t: Councilor Ruiz shrugged at “I just know” and smiled at a number from a tool, because she could check it herself.
Every station needs a source, a receiver and a way to collect evidence. Without a tool, a station is NOT READY.
Your hands can be fooled: the same water felt warm AND cool. A measurement, checked by someone else, made the evidence PROVEN.

clues.where: The Lesson, Part 4: run the stations
clues.t: At every station the receiver changed, and a tool measured it: 104°F to 92°F, a 6 cm to 12 cm light spot, rice jumping 1 cm and 4 cm, 250 lux to 0.

solve.title: What will convince Councilor Ruiz?
solve.q: Which answer fits all four clues?

options.t: Tell her Sam is an engineer, so she should trust him.
options.why: Check Clue 1. Being an expert isn’t evidence she can check.

options.t: Describe how each station looked and felt.
options.why: Check Clue 3. Hands can be fooled. What makes evidence strong?

options.t: Run four stations, each with a source, a receiver and a tool, and bring her observations AND measurements she can check.
options.why: Case cracked! Now present your evidence to the town council, just below.

options.t: Wait for another lightning storm and hope she sees it.
options.why: Check Clue 4. You can collect evidence right now with stations.

doubter.title: Convince the doubter
todo: Tap the evidence you think would convince Councilor Ruiz.
Watch her face. Convince her about all 3.

why.t: Someone who won’t believe a claim until they see evidence. Good scientists are doubters too!

doubter.name: Councilor Ruiz
doubter.halfLine: That’s real evidence! But she wants something she can check herself. Try another card.
doubter.zeroLine: She doesn’t buy it. Pick evidence she could check.
doubter.doneSay: Numbers I can check. Okay, I believe you!

claims.t: This cup of cocoa is warm.

opts.t: I can see steam coming off it.
opts.react: Steam is a clue… but HOW warm?

opts.t: A thermometer in it reads 130°F.
opts.react: A number! I can check that myself.

opts.t: I just know it is.
opts.react: You just KNOW? That’s not evidence.

claims.t: That lamp across the room is sending out light.

opts.t: Lamps always do that.
The wall next to it looks brighter.
opts.react: Brighter to YOU. How much brighter?

opts.t: A light meter by the wall reads 300 with the lamp on and 20 with it off.
opts.react: On, off, two numbers. Now I see it!

claims.t: The tapping pencil is making sound.

opts.t: A sound meter reads 60 while it taps and 35 when it stops.
opts.react: Louder while it taps. I can test that!

opts.t: Everybody knows pencils are noisy.
I can hear tap, tap, tap.
opts.react: You heard it. Can you show me a number?

doubter.q: What convinced Councilor Ruiz the most?

opts.t: A number from a tool, because she could check it herself.
Saying “I just know.”
opts.miss: Look at her face when you picked that one!

opts.t: Whatever sounded the most sure.
opts.miss: Sounding sure isn’t evidence. What could she check?

doubter.win: Numbers she could check won every time. Clue 1!

bulletin.title: Councilor Ruiz speaks
todo: Press Play and listen. You can read along.
Tap the 3 weak spots in her argument.
lines: This is Councilor Ruiz. I read Sam Park’s report about the pier.
Honestly, his chart [[feel|just feels wrong to me]].
Everybody knows [[wire|energy can’t move without wires]].
And I [[look|didn’t even need to look at his numbers]]. [[x:That part is fair! Good scientists DO ask for evidence. Look for the weak spots.|Prove it to me with evidence I can check]].

dangers.does: light and sound cross the air
she didn’t look at the numbers

bulletin.win: Three weak spots! A feeling, a wrong idea and skipped data. Sam has work to do.

stationkit.afterText: Every station has the same three parts
stationkit.title: Build-a-station kit
todo: Drag each part onto its station mat (or tap a part, then a slot).
Every mat needs a source, a receiver and an evidence tool.
Watch out: two parts don’t belong anywhere.

why.t: A tool that measures something and gives you a number, like a thermometer, a ruler or a light meter.

parts.miss: Never a wall outlet! It’s far too strong to play with. A small battery is safe.
That’s not a tool! A station needs a way to collect evidence someone else can check.

parts.t: The cooler air around the cup

stationkit.trayLabel: Parts (drag one onto a mat, or tap it and then a slot)
stationkit.notReady: NOT READY: no way to measure
stationkit.roleMiss: Right station! But this is the {is}, not the {slot}.
stationkit.q: Why does every station need an evidence tool?

opts.t: So we can collect a measurement someone else can check.
Tools make the station look cool.
opts.miss: They do look cool! But what does a tool GIVE you?

opts.t: Without a tool, the energy can’t move.
opts.miss: Energy moves either way. The tool lets us measure it.

stationkit.win: Four stations, each with a source, a receiver and a tool. Clue 2!

proofmeter.afterText: The strongest investigation reports use BOTH
proofmeter.title: Hands lie, numbers don’t
todo: Try the three bowls with the buttons. (You can try it at home with an adult: warm tap water only.)
Then drag (or tap) evidence onto the claim until the meter says PROVEN.

why.t: Your skin feels warmer or cooler than what it touched just before. It can’t tell you an exact temperature.

steps: Put your left hand in the warm bowl and your right hand in the ice water
Move both hands into the middle bowl
proofmeter.thermo: The middle bowl is 72°F. One number.
proofmeter.trickWhy: Your hands only feel warmer or cooler than before. A thermometer gives a number anyone can check.
proofmeter.claim: The cup of cocoa cooled down.

pieces.t: My hand said the mug felt less warm.
pieces.why: Remember the bowls? Hands can be fooled.
A number! But one reading can’t show a change.
An observation anyone could see. A good start!
Being sure isn’t evidence. What could someone check?
Before and after: the number dropped 20°F.
Someone else checked and got the same number.

opts.t: An observation AND a measurement someone else can check.
Whatever your hand feels.
opts.miss: Remember the bowls! The same water felt warm and cool.

opts.t: Saying it very loudly.
opts.miss: Loud isn’t proof. What can someone check?

proofmeter.win: Hands can be fooled, but numbers can be checked. Clue 3!

stationrun.afterText: Now run all four stations yourself
stationrun.title: Run the stations
todo: Press a button to run it.
Read the tool: tap the number it shows. Do both buttons at every station.

why.t: A table where scientists write what they observed and what they measured, so anyone can check it later.

stationrun.readQ: Read the tool. Tap the number it shows ({unit}).
stationrun.pickLine: Press a button above to run the station.
stationrun.lowLine: A little low. Look again where the tool points.
stationrun.highLine: A little high. Look again where the tool points.

stations.safety: Warm tap water only. Never boiling water.

conds.note: A cup of warm tap water just went on the table. The air in the room is 75°F.
Ten minutes later. Heat has been moving from the warm water into the cooler air.

stations.obs: A bright spot on the paper. Farther away, it got bigger and dimmer.
stations.safety: Never shine a flashlight into anyone’s eyes.

conds.note: The light makes a bright spot. How wide is it?
Twice as far away. The spot spreads out and looks dimmer.

stations.obs: The rice grains jumped. Harder taps made them jump higher.
stations.safety: Tap with your hand, not a hard object.

conds.note: A soft tap makes the drum shake a little. How high did the rice jump?
A hard tap sends more energy into the drum.

stations.obs: The bulb glowed. With a wire unhooked, it went dark.
stations.safety: One AA battery and a small bulb. Never a wall outlet.

conds.note: A light meter measures how much light reaches it, in units called lux.
The path is broken. What does the light meter say now?

stationrun.q: At every station, what showed that energy moved?

opts.t: The receiver changed, and a tool measured the change.
Nothing really moved. It was a trick.
opts.miss: Look at your log. Did the numbers change?

opts.t: Only the heat station worked.
opts.miss: Check your log. Did every station get a number?

stationrun.win: Four stations, eight measurements. Your log is ready for the council. Clue 4!

council.title: Present to the council
todo: Councilor Ruiz has one question for each station.
Answer with the evidence that will convince her.
council.lockLine: Crack the case first. Then the council meets.
council.name: Councilor Ruiz
council.answerQ: Answer her with evidence from your station log:

objections.t: Maybe that water was never warm in the first place.
objections.meas: The thermometer read 104°F, then 92°F ten minutes later.
objections.weak: Steam is nice, but how warm was it? She wants a number.
objections.strong: Heat: 104°F → 92°F. Heat moved into the air.

objections.t: Light doesn’t really GO anywhere. It just sits in the flashlight.
objections.obs: I saw a bright spot on the paper.
objections.meas: The spot was 6 cm wide at 20 cm and 12 cm wide at 40 cm.
objections.weak: You saw it, but could she check it? Give her a measurement.
objections.strong: Light: the spot grew from 6 cm to 12 cm as it traveled farther.

objections.t: Tapping a drum can’t move anything else.
objections.meas: The rice jumped 1 cm on a soft tap and 4 cm on a hard tap.
objections.strong: Sound: the rice jumped 1 cm, then 4 cm.

objections.t: That bulb could be a fake. Maybe it glows by itself.
objections.meas: The light meter read 250 lux hooked up and 0 lux unhooked.
objections.weak: Looked bright to YOU. She needs something she can check.

My friend said the bulb was on.

welcome.label: Welcome · prove it to the council
welcome.script: Good news and bad news. The town might pay for a lightning rod on the pier, but Councilor Ruiz doesn’t believe my readings. Read her note. She wants evidence she can check herself. Let’s give her some!

warmup.label: Warm-Up · convince the doubter (Clue 1)
warmup.script: Councilor Ruiz is a tough doubter. For each claim, pick the evidence that would convince her. Watch her face. Does she raise an eyebrow, or does she smile?

vocab.label: Word Wall
vocab.notes: Hold up a thermometer for “measurement”; point at a lamp for “receiver”.

part1.label: Part 1 · build-a-station kit (Clue 2)
part1.script: Every station needs three parts. Drag a source, a receiver, and an evidence tool onto each mat. Watch out for parts that don’t belong. A station without a tool says not ready.

part2.label: Part 2 · hands lie, numbers don’t (Clue 3)
part2.script: Try the three bowls. One hand goes in warm water, one in ice water. Then both go into the middle bowl. Your hands disagree! Next, add evidence to the claim until the meter says proven.

explore.label: Part 4 · run the stations (Clue 4)
explore.script: Time to run all four stations. Pick a station, press a button to run it, then read the tool. Tap the number it shows. Every reading goes into your station log.

assignment.label: Assignment · crack the case
assignment.script: Do you have all four clues? Crack the case at the top of this tab, then present your evidence to the council. After that, answer two questions, write two station reports, and finish your C-E-R.

evidence.label: Use your evidence · CER
evidence.script: A classmate says you can’t really prove that energy moved. Hmm. Think about your thermometer and your rice ruler. Pick your side, tap two pieces of evidence, then explain how they prove your claim.

closing.label: Case closed
closing.script: Case closed! Councilor Ruiz approved the lightning rod, all because of your evidence. Next week, things start crashing. What happens to energy when objects collide?

hlCoach.title: Highlight like a scientist
tips: Highlight key words, not whole paragraphs.
If everything is yellow, nothing stands out. Aim for a few words in each paragraph.
Look for words that are explained.
Bold words, and words followed by “means”, “is called” or a meaning in ( ), are often worth saving.
Look for answers to the Big Question.
Ask yourself: does this help me explain what evidence shows that energy moved?
“Because”, “so” and “first … then” show how ideas connect.
Yellow = important. Green = evidence I might use in my answer. Pink = something I wonder about.

practice.q: Practice: tap the 3 to 5 words that matter most in this sentence.
practice.text: A measurement is a number from a tool that someone else can check.
practice.model: A scientist might highlight “measurement”, “number from a tool” and “someone else can check”. Those words hold the big idea. Small words like “a” and “that” don’t carry the idea.

hlCoach.outside: This works in every subject. When you read anything, save the words that answer your question, and skip the rest.
